# Clinical Health Services

The Veterinary Clinical Complex and Teaching Veterinary Clinical Complex (TVCC) serves the society by providing therapeutic, diagnostic and consultancy services to farmers, animal owners, Animal Husbandry Departments of the country, Forest Department and other Govt Agencies, Military and paramilitary establishments and NGOs. The RVP provide 24X7 emergency services to animal owners and farmers to up-lift the image of the Institute in the society. The polyclinic has earned reputation by its sophisticated facilities and super-specialized therapeutic services for management of hepato-biliary disorders, skin affections, diabetes, management of fracture and other musculoskeletal conditions, urolithiasis, dystocia, infertility, ophthalmic conditions, dental problems, cancer diagnosis and treatment and stem cell therapy for spinal problems and arthritis, etc. The major diagnostic and treatment facilities available in RVP include–Radiography, Ultrasonography, Clinical biochemistry and haematology, Blood, urine and fecal examination, endoscopy, laparoscopy, image intensifier, echocardiography, Haemodialysis, modular operation theatre, obstetrical services, animal lifting facility, indoor facilities for large and small animals etc. Following services are available at RVP.

# Open veterinary clinical trials are currently recruiting

The Cornell University Hospital for Animals is actively engaged in clinical studies that work towards applicable treatments and cures for our patients. Please consider informing owners of eligible patients about relevant studies, and help us move the research forward!

#### Featured Trial:  Pain treatment for canine cancer patients

  * BACKGROUND: Some dogs with cancer, especially end-stage cancer patients or patients with dermatitis secondary to radiation therapy, experience pain that cannot be adequately controlled with oral medications given by their owners at home. Depending on the site of pain, an epidural injection can provide pain relief superior to oral medications, sometimes with fewer side effects. The duration of pain relief is variable but may last several weeks. Repeating the injection requires heavy sedation or general anesthesia each time, and this puts the dog at risk for anesthetic complications, is time consuming, and can be prohibitively expensive.

# Veterinary Clinical Trials

Clinical trials at VROC help evaluate new cancer treatments for pets by assessing their safety, effectiveness, and potential side effects. Participation is entirely voluntary, and the decision to enroll your pet is yours. However, enrollment in a clinical trial is required for a patient to be seen in our clinic.

Our studies build upon the current standard of care using the same advanced technologies available in leading specialty pet cancer hospitals. While specific outcomes cannot be guaranteed, our team is committed to providing the highest standard of veterinary oncology care throughout each trial.

For questions or to learn more about available studies, please contact Paige Neumann, Research Study Coordinator, at 214-645-6221 or by VROC@UTSouthwestern.edu (no-reply@utsouthwestern.edu).

## Study title

Engaging the Immune System to Kill Solid Tumors in Pet Dogs - A Comparative Oncology Approach (TriKE + Radiation Therapy)

## Purpose of study

The purpose of the study is to identify a safe and effective dose of a novel immunotherapy drug (TriKE) when given with hypofractionated radiation therapy (RT) in companion dogs with a sarcoma. 

## Eligibility criteria

Dogs must: 

  * Have cytologically or histopathologicaly confirmed sarcoma, measuring at least 2cm
  * Weigh at least 7 kg (15 lbs)
  * Modified performance score less than 2 and expected survival of at least 2 months

# SBRT for Canine Lung Tumor Study

  * Recruiting
  * Dog
  * Oncology

Primary pulmonary carcinomas in dogs are most commonly treated with surgery, which can result in survival times of approximately one year. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) is a highly precise form of radiation therapy that delivers high doses of radiation directly to a tumor while minimizing exposure to surrounding normal tissues. The purpose of this study is to evaluate dogs with primary pulmonary carcinoma treated using a standardized SBRT protocol across institutions participating in the Veterinary Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (VRTOG).

## Inclusion Criteria

Dogs are eligible for enrollment if they meet all of the following criteria:

  * Cytologic or histopathologic diagnosis of a single primary pulmonary carcinoma.
  * Primary lung tumor measuring greater than 1 cm in its shortest diameter.
  * No previous treatment for the lung tumor.
  * No diagnosis of another malignant tumor outside the lungs within 30 days before enrollment.

The University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine is currently recruiting cats diagnosed with oral carcinomas for a clinical research trial.
